title: Fractures and Open Fractures
disclaimer: FiveM role-play educational guide. This content is not a substitute for clinical training or local trauma protocols. In a real emergency, call 999 or 112.
incident_description: Educational overview of suspected fractures and open fractures, including assessment, neurovascular checks, immobilisation, escalation and documentation.
scene_safety: Follow <C>ABCDE if there is significant trauma.
Control life-threatening bleeding before detailed limb assessment.
Avoid unnecessary manipulation of a suspected fracture.
Do not repeatedly probe or explore an open wound.
mechanism_questions: Direct blow, twisting, crush or axial loading
Contamination with soil, water, sewage or animal material
Ability to move or weight-bear before immobilisation
initial_impression: Consider a fracture with pain, point tenderness, swelling, bruising, loss of function, inability to weight-bear, reduced movement or deformity.
An open fracture should be presumed when there is a wound near a fracture until proven otherwise.
Do not repeatedly manipulate a suspected fracture to confirm it.
Imaging must not delay treatment of life-threatening haemorrhage, vascular compromise or a threatened limb.

catastrophic_haemorrhage: Escalate uncontrolled bleeding or threatened limb.
airway: Follow <C>ABCDE where significant trauma is present.
breathing: Assess for associated chest injury in major trauma.
circulation: Assess pulse, colour, temperature, capillary refill and bleeding.
Look for expanding haematoma or limb ischaemia.
Hard vascular signs include absent palpable pulse, continued significant blood loss and expanding haematoma.
disability: Assess sensation and motor function in relevant nerve territories.
Record altered sensation, weakness or paralysis.
exposure_and_environment: Inspect skin integrity and wounds while maintaining dignity and warmth.
Look for open fracture, deformity and contamination.

required: Distal pulse where a limb injury is present
trend_rules: Document neurovascular assessment before and after realignment, reduction or splinting.
For RP use, require a second neurovascular assessment after any splint, reduction or movement.

fracture_findings: Deformity, angulation, shortening or abnormal rotation
Abnormal movement at the injury site
sensory: Sensation in relevant nerve territories compared with the uninjured limb
motor: Active movement and weakness where safe and appropriate

critical: Suspected femoral shaft fracture with possible haemorrhagic shock
Suspected pelvic fracture with internal bleeding

closed_fracture: Remove rings, watches and restrictive clothing early if swelling is expected.
Support and immobilise the limb in the position found.
Assess and document neurovascular status before and after splinting.
Provide appropriate analgesia according to the authorised protocol.
Arrange imaging and definitive orthopaedic assessment.
Escalate immediately for deformity, neurovascular compromise, severe pain or high-energy mechanism.
open_fracture: Do not push exposed bone back into the wound.
Do not repeatedly inspect, probe or manipulate the wound.
Remove only obvious gross contamination if necessary.
Cover with sterile saline-soaked gauze and an occlusive dressing.
Do not perform a pre-hospital or emergency-department mini-washout of long-bone, hindfoot or midfoot open fractures before formal wound excision.
Give IV prophylactic antibiotics as soon as possible, preferably within 1 hour of injury, without delaying transport; exact regimen follows local trauma-network protocol.
Realign and splint if necessary, particularly with vascular compromise or gross deformity.
Repeat and record neurovascular findings after realignment or splinting.
Arrange urgent orthopaedic and plastic-surgery/orthoplastic review where appropriate.
investigations: Plain radiographs are usually the initial test for an isolated suspected fracture.
Image the joint above and below where clinically relevant.
CT is particularly important for complex, intra-articular, pelvic or multiple injuries.
In adults with blunt major trauma and suspected multiple injuries, whole-body CT may be appropriate according to the major-trauma pathway.
Do not delay life-saving treatment for imaging.

required: Repeat neurovascular assessment after splinting, reduction, realignment or movement.
Monitor for worsening pain, sensory change, weakness or vascular compromise.
compartment_syndrome: Maintain particular awareness for at least 48 hours after tibial fracture or fixation, with regular documented assessments.
Pulselessness, paralysis and marked pallor are late findings; a palpable pulse does not exclude compartment syndrome.

escalation_criteria: Complicated fracture with chest, abdominal, head or spinal injury

open_fracture: Suspected open fractures of long bones, hindfoot or midfoot require direct transfer to a major trauma or specialist centre able to provide orthoplastic care according to the supplied NICE reference.
Hand, wrist, forefoot and digit injuries may follow a different local pathway.
closed_fracture: Arrange imaging and definitive orthopaedic assessment.
Escalate immediately for deformity, neurovascular compromise, severe pain or high-energy mechanism.
